title: Constraint elimination and logical deduction
transcript: In a deduction puzzle, each clue rules out some possibilities. Put positions and candidates in view so that you can see what a clue changes. Combine clues about the same position or person. A small forced block can determine most of the arrangement.

AMC practice may ask who finished first or which option has to be true. Build a short order diagram and mark fixed positions. A Rossmoyne style puzzle may ask for a unique arrangement. Show where the alternatives fail before checking that the survivor works.
Three people line up. Grace is not at either end. Hugo stands before Grace. In what order do Grace, Hugo and Ivy stand? Start with the clue that fixes an exact position.
Grace must go in position two. The only position earlier than two is position one, so Hugo goes there. The final position takes Ivy. Check the order obeys both clues.
Arrange Grace, Hugo, Ivy and Jack in four positions. Hugo is immediately after Grace, and Jack is at one end. Ivy is first. What is the only order?

Ivy is first, so Jack cannot use that end and must be fourth. The remaining two positions are two and three. Put Grace in two and Hugo in three, because Hugo immediately follows Grace. That fixes every name.

Five distinct short films have numbered places one to five, with names Finn, Grace, Hugo, Ivy and Jack. Hugo is immediately before Ivy, and Grace is two places before Ivy. Jack is at one end and earlier than Grace. Finn is not in position two. Find the complete order.

The first two clues force a consecutive block in the order Grace, Hugo, Ivy. Because Jack is before the block and at an end, Jack can only be first. The block can start in position two or three. Starting in three leaves position two for Finn, which the last clue excludes. Start at two. The final order is Jack, Grace, Hugo, Ivy and Finn.

The gap between Grace and Ivy is two places and Hugo sits immediately before Ivy. Jack is first, before Grace, and Finn is fifth. The block had just two starting positions after the end clue. One failed, so the order that passed is unique.

Immediately before means the two positions touch. Earlier than only compares order, so a gap between the names can still be allowed. Finish by checking the arrangement against the original constraints. A solution may look plausible even when it violates an exclusion.

Turn each clue into a fixed place, order or distance. Apply the strongest clues to shrink the possible positions first. If more than one case remains, write each one and identify the clue that accepts or rejects it. Verify the final survivor.
